Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette:
Roimata Parata was fifty-three years old when the delivery truck hit him. He had been a financial analyst for twenty-eight years by then, a Samoan-New Zealand immigrant who had built a steady, predictable life in Portland—a career managing portfolios, a marriage of thirty years to his wife Aroha, a reputation at his firm for precision and calm judgment. The accident happened on a rain-slicked Tuesday in October as he crossed the parking lot of a grocery store, his arms full of bags. The truck's driver had misjudged the turn. Roimata heard the engine sound first—a heavy, accelerating growl—before he felt the impact that threw him across the asphalt. His ribs fractured. His left leg broke in two places. He lay there smelling the hot rubber of the tires, the acrid diesel fumes, his own blood mixing with rain and wet concrete. The driver's door opened with a metallic screech. Someone screamed. For what felt like hours but was probably minutes, Roimata remained conscious, waiting to know if he would die, listening to the chaos of voices and sirens that seemed to come from inside his own chest.

The physical recovery took fourteen months. The psychological one never really began, because Roimata never quite accepted that what happened to him was over. By the time he returned to work, he had already developed a habit of checking the fire exits in every room before he sat down—a quick visual scan that had become automatic, something he did without thinking, the way other men might adjust their glasses. At the office, he positioned his desk so that his back was never fully to the door. His colleagues assumed he was simply being cautious; they did not notice that his eyes were always moving, always cataloging the space around him, always aware of where the nearest exit lay. He had come to believe that constant vigilance was the only thing standing between himself and catastrophe. You could not relax. You could not let your guard down. The world had shown him what happened when you were simply crossing a parking lot, minding your own business, believing yourself safe.

The smells were worse than he had expected. Diesel fuel, which he encountered occasionally in parking lots or near delivery bays, would stop him mid-breath. His body would flood with adrenaline before his mind had even registered what he was smelling—his heart rate spiking, his palms going cold, his leg muscles tensing as though preparing to run or fight. The smell of hot rubber came later, triggered by worn tires or the friction of a car braking hard nearby. Aroha noticed that he had begun avoiding certain routes to the grocery store, certain parking lots altogether. When she asked him why, he could not quite articulate it. It was not rational. He knew, intellectually, that the probability of being hit again was vanishingly small. But his body did not believe what his mind knew. His body reacted first, always first, flooding him with certainty of danger before conscious thought could intervene. The auditory triggers were perhaps the most insidious. Car sounds—the acceleration of an engine, the screech of tires, even the ordinary rumble of traffic—could transport him instantly back to that parking lot. The memory would arrive complete and overwhelming, not as something he was remembering but as something that was happening right now, in the present tense. He would hear the truck engine again, that terrible growl, and the memory would carry not just the visual image but the actual sounds, as though his ears were hearing them afresh. At night, he began waking in the dark, his body rigid with vigilance, needing to verify that he was safe, that Aroha was beside him, that the bedroom door was still locked.

Darkness had become a problem too. He could not enter a dark room without turning on every light. The parking garage at his office building made him nauseated. He had started arriving at work earlier and earlier, parking in the daylit areas near the entrance, accepting the longer walk rather than risk the shadowed levels below. But what had begun as avoidance of places had slowly become avoidance of thought itself. In the weeks after the accident, whenever the memory threatened to surface—when he was alone in the car, or in those vulnerable moments before sleep—Roimata would deliberately redirect his attention. He would turn up the radio, call Aroha, open his work email, anything to keep his mind from settling on what had happened. If he allowed himself to really think about it, to sit with the full weight of that moment, he was certain he would not be able to handle it. The memory would consume him entirely, pull him under, and he would lose himself in the panic and the helplessness. It was safer to keep moving, to keep his mind occupied, to treat the memory as something that must never be examined directly. Aroha had gently suggested therapy six months ago. He had refused. To talk about it with a stranger, to deliberately recall those details—the sounds, the pain, the certainty of death—felt like voluntarily stepping back into the path of the truck.

He is now sixty-three. Last month, he had a panic attack at his desk when a colleague's car backfired in the parking lot below. He left work at two in the afternoon and did not return for a week. His supervisor had begun making quiet inquiries about his reliability. Aroha finally insisted. She told him she was frightened of losing him, not to the truck, but to the life he had stopped living—the grocery trips they took together, the evening drives to the coast, even the simple act of sitting in a room without scanning for exits. This week, for the first time, Roimata made an appointment with a therapist. He is terrified of what it will mean to stop being vigilant, to stop believing that constant guard is the only thing keeping him alive. But he is more terrified still of the alternative—a life shrinking further with each passing month, until there is nothing left to protect.

missing.item: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
missing.explanation: The vignette includes the avoidance cognition ('If he thought about the event, really thought about it, he is certain he would not be able to handle it'), but this is presented as Roimata's own stated belief. However, the symptom item 'Thought Avoidance' specifically refers to a reported behavioral/cognitive pattern where the patient avoids thinking about the event due to fear of being overwhelmed. While the vignette contains the underlying thought, it does not clearly demonstrate that Roimata is actively avoiding thinking about the event as a coping strategy—only that he holds this belief. The distinction is subtle but clinically important: the symptom reflects active avoidance behavior motivated by this fear, not merely the presence of the fear itself.
